entries.title: Registran la quinta muerte relacionada con el calor en el área de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>La muerte de una mujer de 47 años del vecindario de Greater Grand Crossing es la quinta persona que ha fallecido, al menos en parte debido al calor desde el 1 de julio en el área de Chicago, dijeron las autoridades el viernes.</p><p>Una autopsia realizada el viernes determinó que la causa principal de la muerte de Stephanie Rodríguez fueron complicaciones ocasionadas por un golpe de calor, según la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook. Una causa secundaria fue la esquizofrenia.</p><p>Rodríguez, residente de la cuadra 700 al oeste de 76th Street, sufrió complicaciones en la intersección al oeste de 53rd Street y al sur de Halsted Street en el vecindario Back of the Yards, de acuerdo con la Oficina del Médico Forense. Rodríguez fue declarada muerta a las 3:52 a.m. del jueves en el Centro Médico de la Universidad de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-880000" name="module-880000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Desde el 1 de julio, otras cuatro personas han fallecido, al menos en parte, debido al calor.</p><p>El 3 de julio murieron Barbara Whigham, de 71 años, y Mike Rodríguez, de 57 años, informaron las autoridades.</p><p>Whigham fue encontrada inconsciente dentro de una residencia en la cuadra 1000 al oeste de 70th Street en Englewood, y aunque su causa principal de muerte fue una enfermedad cardíaca, las causas contribuyentes incluyeron asma, obesidad y estrés por calor, según la oficina.</p><p>Rodríguez, quien fue hallado inconsciente en una casa en la cuadra 3200 al sur de Archer Avenue en el vecindario McKinley Park, murió principalmente debido a una enfermedad cardíaca, con factores como la diabetes y el estrés por calor contribuyendo a su fallecimiento, dijo la oficina del médico forense.</p><p>El 2 de julio, David González, de 44 años, fue encontrado inconsciente en una residencia en la cuadra 2700 al oeste de 68th Street en Chicago Lawn por oficiales que respondían a una investigación de muerte. González fue declarado muerto el 4 de julio, y una autopsia determinó que la causa de la muerte fue principalmente un golpe de calor. Las causas contribuyentes a su muerte fueron: enfermedad cardíaca, diabetes y obesidad.</p><p>El 1 de julio, Daniel Machnikowski, de 69 años, falleció tras ser hallado en su hogar en la cuadra 1200 de Darrow Street en el suburbio norte de Evanston. Machnikowski murió principalmente de una enfermedad cardíaca, con el estrés por calor listado como una causa secundaria, informó la oficina del médico forense.</p><p>Las cinco muertes ocurrieron después de que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/29/heat-wave-chicago-area-city-services" target="_blank" >los funcionarios de salud advirtieron</a> que los períodos prolongados de calor extremo pueden ser especialmente peligrosos para los adultos mayores, las personas con condiciones médicas crónicas y para quienes no tienen acceso confiable al aire acondicionado.</p><p>Actualmente, Chicago cuenta con <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/30/chicago-heat-wave-extreme-weather-brandon-johnson-health-south-side-west-side" target="_blank" >287 instalaciones de enfriamiento disponibles en toda la ciudad</a> para los residentes que buscan alivio, incluyendo todos los 22 distritos de policía, centros de servicios comunitarios, las Bibliotecas Públicas de Chicago, centros de enfriamiento del Distrito de Parques de Chicago y centros para personas mayores, según una declaración anterior de la oficina del alcalde Brandon Johnson.</p><p>Los seis Centros de Servicios Comunitarios estarán abiertos para el enfriamiento durante el horario de operación estándar, de 9 a.m. a 5 p.m., los días de semana.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: In first Midway Blitz sentencing, feds want 30-month prison term for man who fired gun near immigration agents
entries.summary: <p>Federal prosecutors are seeking a<b> </b>2½-year prison sentence<b> </b>for the man who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/27/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-little-village-trump-bovino" target="_blank" >admitted firing<b> </b>a gun</a> “in proximity of”<b> </b>U.S. Customs and Border Protection<b> </b>agents last fall<b> </b>in the waning days of Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>Hector Gomez, 46, is one of only two people convicted of a non-immigration crime tied to the Trump administration’s deportation campaign in the Chicago area last year. Gomez<b> </b>pleaded<b> </b>guilty<b> </b>in April<b> </b>to<b> </b>illegally<b> </b>possessing<b> </b>a firearm<b> </b>as a felon.</p><p>Gomez, who was born<b> </b>in Mexico<b> </b>and has no lawful status<b> </b>in the United States, is set to be sentenced July 20<b> </b>by<b> </b>U.S. District Judge<b> </b>Matthew<b> </b>Kennelly. Gomez’s attorneys<b> </b>have sought a brief delay.</p><p>They are seeking an 18-month<b> </b>sentence<b> </b>and acknowledge<b> </b>that he's likely to be deported<b> </b>once he finishes his prison time.</p><p>Federal prosecutors have charged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >33 known defendants</a> with non-immigration crimes tied to Midway Blitz. Twenty-four<b> </b>were cleared, and five are on track to see their charges dismissed. Charges against two others<b> </b>are still pending.</p><p>The claim that agents had been fired upon in early November was met with skepticism, especially when no charges were initially announced against an alleged shooter. Then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b>told Fox News<b> </b>a suspect had been found "within 48 hours."</p><p>But, in a recent court filing, Gomez’s lawyers wrote that he<b> </b>fired<b> </b>his<b> </b>weapon<b> </b>as<b> </b>agents<b> </b>“arrested members of Mr. Gomez’s community in Little Village.”</p><p>“Evidence shows that Mr. Gomez’s discharge of a firearm was in an upward trajectory," attorneys Michael<b> </b>Monaco<b> </b>and<b> </b>Kathleen<b> </b>Dorsey<b> </b>wrote. “That is, any shots fired were pointed above the heads of CBP agents and any other community members present, and not in the direction of any person.”</p><p>They also wrote that the incident took place during<b> </b>one<b> </b>of<b> </b>multiple<b> </b>“binge-drinking”<b> </b>episodes<b> </b>Gomez has experienced since<b> </b>he<b> </b>began<b> </b>drinking<b> </b>at 14. They said he told them “he had been drinking the night before until 2 or 3 in the morning, and started drinking again immediately upon waking the morning of November 8.”</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Jill<b> </b>Bhalakia<b> </b>wrote that Gomez<b> </b>purchased a beer<b> </b>that morning. Then, a little more than<b> </b>an hour later, driving a black<b> </b>Jeep<b> </b>Wrangler, he fired<b> </b>at least two rounds<b> </b>near<b> </b>Border Patrol agents around the 2400 block<b> </b>of South Kedzie Avenue. The area was “busy with pedestrians, vehicles and CBP agents actively engaged in law enforcement activity,”<b> </b>she wrote.</p><p>Gomez<b> </b>fled<b> </b>but<b> </b>parked<b> </b>nearby, around<b> </b>the<b> </b>3100 block<b> </b>of West 26th Street, the prosecutor wrote. Then, around<b> </b>2:30 p.m., she<b> </b>said<b> </b>Gomez<b> </b>got out of the Jeep and<b> </b>brandished<b> </b>the<b> </b>gun<b> </b>in front of an unnamed<b> </b>victim, “laughing profusely”<b> </b>as he did so.</p><p>The Chicago police<b> </b>later<b> </b>found<b> </b>the<b> </b>gun<b> </b>in<b> </b>Gomez’s<b> </b>lap<b> </b>as<b> </b>he<b> </b>sat<b> </b>in<b> </b>the<b> </b>vehicle’s<b> </b>driver’s<b> </b>seat<b> </b>“near beer bottles in the center console,”<b> </b>according<b> </b>to<b> </b>Bhalakia.</p><p>Bhalakia wrote that Gomez<b> </b>has been removed<b> </b>from the United States<b> </b>“on multiple occasions,”<b> </b>has a 2010<b> </b>illegal<b> </b>entry<b> </b>conviction<b> </b>and was the subject<b> </b>of<b> </b>a<b> </b>final<b> </b>order<b> </b>of<b> </b>removal<b> </b>on<b> </b>Dec. 10. He also was convicted<b> </b>last year<b> </b>of aggravated<b> </b>unlawful<b> </b>possession<b> </b>of a weapon.</p><p>Monaco and Dorsey wrote that Gomez<b> </b>was born<b> </b>in a rural area of Mexico and<b> </b>was<b> </b>kidnapped in 2008 or 2009 along<b> </b>with<b> </b>his<b> </b>father<b> </b>and<b> </b>youngest<b> </b>sister<b> </b>and<b> </b>held<b> </b>for<b> </b>ransom. His family sold their belongings<b> </b>to pay the ransom, according to the his lawyers.</p><p>He is now married, and his wife<b> </b>lives<b> </b>in<b> </b>Mexico<b> </b>and cares for their<b> </b>three<b> </b>children, according to Monaco and Dorsey. They<b> </b>called him a “hardworking member of his community”<b> </b>who has worked at Mexican restaurants and done odd jobs<b> </b>to support his family.</p><p>Bhalakia argued that Gomez’s<b> </b>crime<b> </b>“not only endangered the community … but also further jeopardized his ability to be present for his wife and children.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/27/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-little-village-trump-bovino" >Man admits opening fire near border agents during Operation Midway Blitz</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/11/20/chicago-border-patrol-ice-midway-blitz-trump-bovino-little-village-shooting-gun-hector-gomez" >Feds haven’t charged anyone with shooting at Border Patrol agents in Chicago despite touting arrest</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/15/crime-chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-ice-border-patrol" >Feds in Chicago get first guilty plea in a Midway Blitz case — but not for assaulting immigration agents</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

all-ages show at Bottom Lounge dubbed “Vocalo’s Summer Meltdown.”</p><p>The fans were responding to Adamn Killa’s call on social media for fans to wear pink — referencing <a class="Link" entries.title: Chicago demuestra ‘esfuerzos ejemplares’ al instalar señales de cruce accesibles para peatones con discapacidad
entries.summary: <p>Un año después de que un juez federal ordenara a Chicago instalar señales de cruces peatonales más accesibles para personas con discapacidad, un auditor designado por la corte encontró que la Ciudad cumplió con los requisitos mínimos al instalar 78 nuevas señales.</p><p>Sin embargo, en su <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/d3/e7/21bd91c14354aaf73233c7276cd6/pedestrian-crossing-monitor-report.pdf" target="_blank" >informe del primer año</a> publicado el 1 de julio, el auditor también encontró que ninguna de las señales accesibles de Chicago que se inspeccionaron —con su distintivo sonido audible— cumple plenamente con los estándares federales actuales.</p><p>"Son utilizables. Pero no son tan efectivas como pueden y deben ser", dijo Rachel M. Weisberg, abogada directora de Disability Rights Advocates, que presentó la demanda original en 2019 que llevó a la designación del auditor Michael G. Shaw en junio de 2025.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b60000" name="module-b60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Las señales, cuando se presionan, emiten un pitido cuando es seguro cruzar la calle para peatones ciegos y con discapacidad visual. Los botones también vibran para alertar a los peatones con discapacidad auditiva sobre un cambio en la señal.</p><p>Los estándares para los pasos peatonales, conocidos como señales accesibles para peatones, son determinados por el Manual de Dispositivos Uniformes para el Control del Tránsito (MUTCD). El manual establece las especificaciones técnicas sobre todo, desde la altura de la colocación de los botones hasta la distancia de la señal con la acera, según destacó Weisberg.</p><p>Además de no cumplir con los requisitos técnicos, el auditor encontró que muchos dispositivos no estaban funcionando correctamente o requerían mantenimiento.</p><p>La Ciudad tiene trabajo por hacer en ese sentido, señaló Weisberg. Pero ha logrado un avance sustancial en la identificación y construcción de señales accesibles en los cruces peatonales de la ciudad.</p><p>En el primer año bajo supervisión judicial, el auditor encontró:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-9ddc62f0-7f0b-11f1-9aec-151a20040bfd"><li>La Ciudad instaló 78 señales accesibles para peatones, ocho más de lo que requería la corte. Los requisitos aumentarán en los próximos años. Se exige a la Ciudad construir señales en 110 intersecciones en el segundo año de la orden correctiva del juez.</li><li>La Ciudad ahora tiene señales accesibles en 165 intersecciones, 6.5% de las 2,800 intersecciones totales en la ciudad.</li><li>El Departamento de Transporte de Chicago "demostró esfuerzos ejemplares" al seguir la orden del juez, y ha redactado una política de señales accesibles para peatones y ha construido varias señales accesibles en intersecciones solicitadas por el público.</li></ul><p>La oficina del alcalde Brandon Johnson dijo que la Ciudad ha aumentado sus intersecciones accesibles en un 90% en el último año y está comprometida a lograr "una plena conformidad operacional".</p><p>"Si bien este trabajo todavía está en sus etapas iniciales y los esfuerzos para abordar las deficiencias técnicas en las señales actuales continúan avanzando, estamos generando un fuerte impulso a medida que expandimos la infraestructura accesible y creamos calles más seguras e inclusivas para todos los residentes", dijo la oficina de Johnson en un comunicado.</p><p>El Departamento de Transporte (CDOT), que instala las señales, disputó la caracterización de que todas sus intersecciones accesibles no cumplían con los requisitos.</p><p>En un comunicado, un portavoz del departamento señaló que una intersección sólo se considera completamente conforme en el informe si se cumplen todos los elementos aplicables de esas listas de verificación. El departamento dijo que el 90% de los elementos individuales de la lista de verificación evaluados se registraron en cumplimiento y que la mayoría de las intersecciones inspeccionadas se completaron antes de que se nombrara al auditor de la corte.</p><p>"La Ciudad ha construido una base sólida para este programa a largo plazo y está comprometida a continuar mejorando y expandiendo (las señales accesibles para los peatones) en Chicago", dijo un portavoz del Departamento de Transporte en un correo electrónico.</p><p>Desde 2019, la Ciudad ha construido señales accesibles en todos los proyectos de reconstrucción de intersecciones, señala el comunicado.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Woman's body found in Back of the Yards trash can
entries.summary: <p>The body of a woman was found in a trash can in an alley in Back of the Yards on Saturday, police said.</p><p>The unidentified woman's body was found around 6:25 p.m. Saturday in a trash can in the 700 block of West 54th Street, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Detectives are investigating, and autopsy results are pending.</p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: St. Sabina community once again grapples with sex abuse allegation against Rev. Pfleger
entries.summary: <p>The St. Sabina Church community is once again torn over a sexual abuse allegation against the flock’s longtime leader, the Rev. Michael Pfleger.</p><p>It’s the fifth decades-old accusation against the South Side priest in four years, though each has ended with Pfleger being cleared by the Archdiocese of Chicago and returning to the helm. Pfleger called the most recent allegations "another attempt by someone to get money from the archdiocese and to silence me."</p><p>Cardinal Blase Cupich announced the accusation and corresponding investigation in a letter Saturday. He recognized church members may be distressed, but asked them to let the investigation conclude, saying the church's policy "has proven effective in protecting the rights of all." </p><p>The Archdiocese Office for Child Abuse Investigations and Review said the allegation was reported to law enforcement, per its policies.</p><p>Angela Walker, executive director of the Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests, suggested that the accuser report their allegations to law enforcement as opposed to the church, which she said has a history of "sweeping accusations under the rug."</p><p>"We really are advocating people go to the authorities," Walker said. "This needs to be treated like a crime."</p><p>Pfleger was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/5/22215973/father-michael-pfleger-removed-st-sabina-sexual-abuse-allegation" target="_blank" >first removed</a> from the pulpit in January 2021 amid separate allegations, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/6/6/22521628/father-pfleger-returns-st-sabina-sex-abuse-allegations" target="_blank" ><u>returning that June</u></a> with a three-hour service where he said his reputation would likely be tarnished to some forever. He was temporarily removed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/15/23406159/father-pfleger-sex-abuse-allegations-misconduct-second-archdiocese-chicago-sabina" target="_blank" ><u>again in October 2022</u></a> before being cleared by the church three months later, when he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/12/10/23503376/pfleger-reinstated-st-sabina-chicago-archdiocese-sex-abuse-allegation-unfounded" target="_blank" ><u>returned again that December</u></a>.</p><p>Three people who previously accused Pfleger of misconduct didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/07/11/michael-pfleger-removed-st-sabina-church-sex-abuse-claim-blaise-cupich-catholic-church" >Rev. Michael Pfleger removed from St. Sabina Church amid investigation into decades-old sex abuse claim</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/12/10/23503376/pfleger-reinstated-st-sabina-chicago-archdiocese-sex-abuse-allegation-unfounded" >Rev. Michael Pfleger reinstated at St. Sabina after review board clears him of latest sex abuse allegation</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/15/23406159/father-pfleger-sex-abuse-allegations-misconduct-second-archdiocese-chicago-sabina" >Rev. Michael Pfleger removed from St. Sabina again as archdiocese investigates another decades-old sex abuse claim</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/6/6/22521628/father-pfleger-returns-st-sabina-sex-abuse-allegations" >Pfleger returns to St. Sabina, reflects on ‘painful nightmare’ that followed sex abuse allegations</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Walker said survivors sometimes struggle to come forward against church officials because they face being doubted by their fellow parishioners.</p><p>"If your church has been a part of your community, it is very challenging" to come forward, Walker said. "Having gone through this trauma, and then not being believed and being attacked, is a horrible thing. Sometimes a community of faithful will rally around the abuser instead of the survivor."</p><p>Some members of St. Sabina told the Chicago Sun-Times they are standing by Pfleger while the investigation proceeds.</p><p>Robin Patterson, 50, attended St. Sabina schools kindergarten through eighth grade and has lived down the street from the church since she was 5 years old. She said, in her experience, Pfleger did not interact with kids much. She echoed Pfleger's previous claim he was being targeted for political and monetary gain.</p><p>“They payin’ somebody to do this again,” Patterson said outside the church Monday afternoon. “They want him out. It’s just a shame. ... I hope he’s cleared and back here soon."</p><p>Rachel Giles, who is part of another parish but occasionally attends St. Sabina events, said she felt the same. The Auburn Gresham resident of seven years said Pfleger’s community marches against gun violence have made an impact, and while other church staff may pick up the mantle in the meantime, she was waiting for an uptick in crime.</p><p>“He does too much good for the community," Giles said. "He’s the last hope we got.”</p><p>Walker, of the Survivors Network, hopes the wider community will start to see the pattern in the repeated allegations and call for action.</p><p>"We're talking about two decades of accusations. And rather than taking this at face value and investigating it and removing him, he's been reinstated," Walker said. "I think the community is going to demand his removal."</p>

entries.title: Finance Committee stalls showdown vote on sale of Chicago parking meters
entries.summary: <p>A City Council committee poised to reject a New York investment firm’s $2.53 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters instead postponed that politically-volatile vote Monday under threat of a lawsuit by the current owner.</p><p>In a July 3 letter to Mayor Brandon Johnson, Finance Chair Pat Dowell warned that the proposal by Chicago Parking Meters LLC to unload the 57 years that remain on the lopsided deal “has not secured the support necessary to advance from committee at this time.”</p><p>Chicago Parking Meters is a consortium that includes Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi. They want to sell the time left on the deal to Stonepeak Partners and have threatened to sue the city if the deal is rejected.</p><p>“Significant questions remain regarding Stonepeak’s ownership structure, regulatory and legal history, operational practices and the potential implications of this transfer for the city of Chicago," Dowell wrote. </p><p>“These are fundamental considerations for any legislative body asked to approve the transfer of a public asset of this magnitude.”</p><p>During Monday’s Finance Committee meeting, Dowell told her colleagues that there would be no vote on the proposal by Stonepeak Partners to acquire Chicago parking meters for what's left of the deal famously engineered in 2008 by then-Mayor Richard M. Daley.</p><p>Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28<sup>th</sup>), the mayor’s most powerful City Council ally, said he hopes to use the delay to push an alternative plan.</p><p>It would create a public infrastructure trust similar to the one created, then abandoned by now former Mayor Rahm Emanuel to acquire the parking meters, using a mix of investments by the four city employee pension funds and municipal bonds.</p><p>“That was then. This is now. We have a meaningful asset that can be utilized, and it also potentially strengthens our pension funds and it works to bring that value back to Chicagoans—not let the money go half-way around the world,” Ervin told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“Other pension funds are investing in this. Why wouldn’t we afford that same opportunity to our four pension funds in the city of Chicago?”</p><p>Johnson ultimately abandoned his $3.2 billion bid to take back Chicago parking meters after determining that the risk of undoing the parking meter deal that Chicagoans love to hate was not worth the reward either financially or politically.</p><p>It would have been required to pledge to siphon other major sources of revenue the city depends on “if parking habits shifted, alternative modes of transportation become more common” and “driver/commuter behaviors” changed.</p><p>That’s a distinct possibility amid a fast-changing landscape for parking demand that includes everything from self-driving vehicles and robot deliveries to congestion fees that discourage people from driving Downtown.</p><p>“If parking meter revenue was not sufficient to cover the principal and interest payments, then spending on other infrastructure projects or critical services would have been impacted,” the mayor’s office memo to the City Council stated.</p><p>Against that backdrop, Ervin was asked Monday to explain how he would bankroll the proposed Infrastructure Trust purchase.</p><p>“If we create an opportunity, there would definitely need to be some financing done by the city….Looking at all options, that would probably include pension obligation bonds, general obligation bonds. Even maybe some revenue bonds along TIF and other things,” Ervin said.</p><p>“It’s just an opportunity that we need to explore, we need to look at and not let this opportunity pass us by.</p><p>The City Council was facing a July 24 deadline to either authorize the sale to Stonepeak or reject it and risk a lawsuit by Chicago Parking Meters LLC, a consortium that includes Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi.</p><p>It’s unclear whether there is any flexibility in that deadline.</p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson warned that Chicago taxpayers would pay a heavy price for rejecting Stonepeak’s $2.53 billion bid.</p><p>“One is a lawsuit on the basis of the no vote because it really puts the city on the precipice of breach. The second is…the city’s reputation as a party with whom the private sector, the investment community, bond purchasers can say actually keeps its word. It is a demonstration of…further volatility that makes the city appear to be a less reliable partner in major financial matters," Ferguson said.</p><p>Ferguson urged the Council to take Stonepeak up on its offer to work with the city to modify that portion of the widely-despised parking meter deal that requires the city to compensate Chicago Parking Meters LLC for every parking space taken out of service either for a special event or construction project.</p><p>“That’s something that could be worth $5 million, $10 million, maybe more a year. And the fact that they’re willing to even look at that suggests that this is a party that understands the history of this deal, the volatile politics around it and actually cares to be something of a good corporate citizen," he said.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman
